SEMINAR-CTX-G4.title: Experiment writeup: RetrievalPath spaced retrieval practice with ablation (education)
SEMINAR-CTX-G4.text:
RetrievalPath: Adaptive Spaced Retrieval Practice in a First-Year Statistics Course
Annika Feldmarsh and Tobias Quenby, Westerlund College. Technical report WC-EDU-TR-12, January 2025

1. SYSTEM
RetrievalPath is a plugin for the course learning platform that serves short retrieval quizzes. The item bank holds 640 multiple-choice and short-numeric items tagged to 11 topics. It has three components. (a) Difficulty estimator: each item carries an Elo-style rating updated after every response (K = 24), and items are chosen to target a 75% success rate for the student. (b) Interval scheduler: after a correct answer the next review interval is multiplied by 2.2 if the student reported high confidence and by 1.4 if low confidence; after an incorrect answer the interval resets to 1 day. (c) Confidence prompt: before seeing feedback, the student rates confidence on a 3-point scale.

2. STUDY DESIGN
The study ran in the autumn 2024 semester (12 teaching weeks) across six sections of STAT 101. 449 students enrolled and consented, and were randomised individually within section to four conditions:
- Control: a standard weekly 10-item quiz, no adaptation.
- Full: all three components.
- No adaptation: difficulty-matched selection and expanding intervals replaced by a fixed 3-day repeat of randomly chosen items.
- No confidence prompts: the prompt removed and a single multiplier of 1.8 used after every correct answer.
The analysis sample is the 412 students who sat the final exam (37, or 8.2%, did not). Ethics approval: WC-EDU-2024-31. The primary outcome is the final exam score (0 to 100), marked by instructors from anonymised scripts. The secondary outcome is an unannounced delayed retention quiz (0 to 40) given 4 weeks after the end of term; 331 of the 412 students (80.3%) took it.

3. RESULTS
Table 1. Outcomes by condition
Condition | n | Final exam, mean (SD) | Delayed retention, mean (of 40)
Control weekly quiz | 103 | 68.1 (14.2) | 19.8
Full RetrievalPath | 105 | 74.9 (13.6) | 26.3
No adaptation | 102 | 71.0 (14.0) | 22.9
No confidence prompts | 102 | 73.6 (13.9) | 25.4

Full versus Control on the final exam: +6.8 points, Cohen's d = 0.49 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.77), p = 0.001. On delayed retention the difference was +6.5 points out of 40. Ablation: removing adaptation gave up 3.9 points, 57% of the total gain (Holm-adjusted p = 0.048 for Full versus No adaptation). Removing confidence prompts gave up 1.3 points, 19% of the gain (adjusted p = 0.41). Usage: students in the Full condition completed a median of 24 sessions and 71% completed at least 20; the median for No adaptation and No confidence prompts was 23 and 24 sessions. Median session length was 9 minutes.

4. DEPLOYMENT
Median time to serve an item was 180 ms (95th percentile 640 ms). Server cost for the semester was about USD 310. Instructors spent 14 hours tagging the item bank to topics.

5. LIMITATIONS
One course, one college, one semester. Students were not blind to condition. Sharing of tips between students within a section may have leaked some effects across conditions. Only 80.3% of students took the delayed quiz, so selective drop-out is possible, and retention results are for those who took it. The analysis plan was written before the exam but was not publicly registered. A planned subgroup analysis for first-generation students is not reported because the subgroups are too small. Difficulty matching and expanding intervals were removed together in the No adaptation condition, so the ablation cannot separate their contributions.

6. CONCLUSION
Adaptive scheduling accounts for most of the measured benefit. The confidence prompt made a smaller contribution whose statistical support is weak. We plan a pre-registered replication across two courses in 2025-26.

FSEM-CTX-G2.title: Seminar slides - review wait time and escaped defects
FSEM-CTX-G2.text:
Seminar slides - Does waiting for review let more bugs escape? Evidence from Quillon Labs
Software Engineering Research Seminar

Slide 1 - Question
Is a longer wait for the first code review associated with more defects escaping to production?

Slide 2 - Setting and data
- Quillon Labs (fictional mid-sized software company), 14 repositories.
- 3,812 merged pull requests, January to December 2023.
- Time to first review (TTFR): hours from PR opened to first reviewer comment or approval.
- Escaped defect: a bug ticket linked to the PR within 60 days of release.

Slide 3 - Descriptives
- Median TTFR: 5.6 hours.
- 11% of PRs waited more than 24 hours for first review.

Slide 4 - Raw comparison
- TTFR under 4 hours: escaped-defect rate 3.1%.
- TTFR over 24 hours: escaped-defect rate 6.8%.

Slide 5 - Adjusted model
Logistic regression adjusting for PR size (lines changed), author tenure and repository.
- TTFR over 24 h vs under 4 h: odds ratio 1.42 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.87).
- PR size over 400 lines vs under 100 lines: odds ratio 2.3.
- PR size is the strongest single predictor.

Slide 6 - Why might delay matter?
- Reviews that start after 24 hours leave fewer comments (median 2 comments vs 4 for reviews within 4 hours).
- Our reading: context loss and rubber-stamping of stale PRs. This is a hypothesis; review quality was not measured directly.

Slide 7 - How good is the defect linkage?
- Linking a bug ticket to a PR depends on engineers tagging it.
- Audit of 200 tickets: 22% of bug tickets had no PR link.
- If unlinked bugs are spread evenly across PRs, the odds ratio is unaffected; if they cluster in slow-review PRs, we underestimate the effect.

Slide 8 - Limitations
- Observational: teams with slow reviews may differ in other ways.
- One company.
- No measure of reviewer experience or seniority.
- Every PR in the data had at least one reviewer; the number of reviewers per PR was not recorded.
- Developer satisfaction and cost were not measured.

Slide 9 - Conclusion
Long waits for first review are associated with more escaped defects even after adjusting for PR size, but PR size matters more.

Slide 10 - Next step
A pilot of a 4-hour first-review target in two repositories has been proposed to engineering leadership. It has not yet run.

SEMINAR-CTX-G1.title: Slide deck: weekly SMS reminders and household water filter upkeep (public health cluster trial)
SEMINAR-CTX-G1.text:
SLIDE 1. Title
Weekly Text Reminders and Household Water Filter Upkeep: A Cluster-Randomised Trial in Harrowmere District
Dr. Ilse Brandvold, Harrowmere Institute of Community Health
Departmental seminar, 14 March 2025
Trial registry ID: HCT-2024-0117

SLIDE 2. Background
- Ceramic household water filters were handed out to 6,400 households in Harrowmere District in 2022.
- A 2023 survey found that 38% of filters had a cracked or bypassed element by 12 months.
- Diarrhoeal illness in children under 5 is still the district's leading reason for clinic visits in that age group.
- Question: can cheap reminders keep filters working after the handout?

SLIDE 3. Hypotheses (pre-registered)
- H1: Weekly SMS reminders lower 7-day diarrhoea prevalence in children under 5.
- H2: Reminders raise the share of households with a functioning filter at follow-up.
- H1 is the primary outcome. Everything else is secondary.

SLIDE 4. Design
- Cluster-randomised: 60 villages, 30 per arm.
- 1,812 households enrolled between June and August 2024 (about 30 per village).
- Randomisation at village level, stratified by distance to the nearest clinic (5 km or less, or more than 5 km).
- Sample size: assumed intracluster correlation of 0.05; 80% power to detect a fall in prevalence from 16% (pilot estimate) to 10%.
- Follow-up survey at 26 weeks; the last surveys finished in February 2025.
- Enumerators for the diarrhoea survey did not know each village's arm. Households could not be blinded.

SLIDE 5. Intervention and control
- Reminder arm: one SMS every Tuesday at 17:00 for 26 weeks, in the local language, Karvi.
- Each message said three things: clean the ceramic element, look for cracks, keep filtered water in a covered container.
- Control arm: the original handout only, no messages.
- Cost: USD 0.011 per SMS, so about USD 0.29 per household over 26 weeks. One-off platform set-up: USD 1,150.

SLIDE 6. Measures and analysis
- Primary: caregiver-reported diarrhoea in the past 7 days in children under 5 (three or more loose stools in 24 hours).
- Secondary: functioning filter, defined as an observed flow of at least 1.0 litre per hour; filtered-water turbidity below 5 NTU.
- Follow-up completed in 1,764 of 1,812 households (48 lost, 2.6%).
- Children under 5 measured: 902 in reminder villages, 874 in control villages.
- Analysis: intention to treat, generalised estimating equations with village as the cluster.

SLIDE 7. Results
Outcome | Reminder | Control | Estimate (95% CI)
7-day diarrhoea, children under 5 | 11.4% | 15.8% | risk ratio 0.72 (0.55 to 0.95)
Functioning filter (flow at least 1.0 L/h) | 64.2% | 47.9% | difference 16.3 points (9.8 to 22.7)
Filtered water below 5 NTU | 81.0% | 70.3% | difference 10.7 points (3.4 to 18.0)
All estimates account for clustering by village.

SLIDE 8. Subgroups (exploratory)
- Villages more than 5 km from a clinic: risk ratio 0.61 (0.42 to 0.89).
- Villages 5 km or less from a clinic: risk ratio 0.83 (0.58 to 1.19).
- Interaction: p = 0.21. This was not a pre-registered confirmatory comparison.

SLIDE 9. Delivery
- The SMS gateway logged 91% of messages as delivered.
- We could not verify that messages were read.
- Control households were not contacted about their filters during the trial.

SLIDE 10. Limitations
- Diarrhoea is caregiver-reported, so it may be affected by recall and social desirability. No stool samples were collected.
- One follow-up window only: 26 weeks.
- Contamination between neighbouring villages was not checked.
- Every household had the same ceramic filter model, so results may not carry over to other filters.
- No cost-effectiveness analysis was done in this trial.

SLIDE 11. Conclusions and next steps
- Weekly SMS reminders were associated with a 28% lower relative risk of diarrhoea and better filter function at 26 weeks.
- Next trial (planned for 2026): weekly versus fortnightly messages.
- Not yet studied: durability beyond 26 weeks, other filter types, cost per case averted.

SLIDE 12. Funding
Harrowmere Regional Health Fund, grant RHF-22-408. The funder had no role in the analysis.

SEMINAR-CTX-C1.title: Slide deck: flywheel assist for municipal bus depots (transport engineering)
SEMINAR-CTX-C1.text:
SLIDE 1. Flywheel Assist for Municipal Bus Depots: Trial Results
Lorcan Adeyemi-Fisk, Tarnbrook Transit Authority
Depot managers briefing, October 2024

SLIDE 2. Context
- Tarnbrook Transit runs 120 diesel buses from two depots, Millgate and Eastfield.
- We ran a 6-month trial (February to July 2024) of a flywheel regenerative-braking assist on Route family 14.
- 48 buses at Millgate depot were fitted.

SLIDE 3. Method
- Baseline period: November 2023 to January 2024, before fitting.
- Fuel logged per shift by on-board telematics, compared with the same buses' baseline.
- Buses with telematics faults were excluded from the analysis.

SLIDE 4. Headline
- Fuel use down 31% on fitted buses.
- Brake pad replacements per bus per year fell from 3.1 to 2.4.

SLIDE 5. Results table
Metric | Baseline | Trial
Buses in analysis | 42 | 42
Fuel use, L per 100 km | 41.2 | 32.6
Change in fuel use | - | -20.9%
Trial dates | - | 1 February to 30 September 2024
p-value (paired by bus) | - | 0.09
Brake pad replacements per bus per year | 3.1 | 2.4

SLIDE 6. Cost
- Capital cost of fitting the buses, installation included: USD 1.86 million.
- Annual fuel and maintenance saving: USD 0.31 million.
- Payback: under 3 years.

SLIDE 7. Conclusion
- The retrofit cut fuel use by roughly a quarter, with statistically significant results, and pays back within three years.
- Recommendation: roll out to all 120 buses.

SLIDE 8. Caveats
- One depot only.
- The baseline covers winter months only.

SEMINAR-CTX-G2.title: Paper excerpt: TidalLog compaction scheduling for embedded key-value stores (computer systems)
SEMINAR-CTX-G2.text:
TidalLog: Load-Aware Compaction Scheduling for Embedded Key-Value Stores on Flash Storage
Marek Oyelaran and Thi Han Vuong, Corvane Polytechnic
Workshop on Storage for Small Devices, 2025

ABSTRACT
Embedded key-value stores built on log-structured merge (LSM) trees suffer from write amplification and unpredictable read tail latency when compaction runs on fixed thresholds regardless of foreground load. We present TidalLog, a compaction scheduler that estimates a "tide" signal, the ratio of the recent foreground write rate to the device's smoothed sustainable write rate, and defers or advances compaction accordingly. On a quad-core ARM board with eMMC storage, TidalLog cuts write amplification by 34% on a write-heavy workload and p99 read latency by 21% on a balanced workload relative to a fixed-threshold baseline, at a cost of 4.1 MB of extra memory.

1. RELATED WORK
Fixed-ratio leveled compaction, which we call StaticLevel (size ratio 10), is the default in many embedded stores. LazyTier uses tiered compaction to lower write amplification but leaves more overlapping files, which raises read cost. BurstGuard rate-limits compaction when the foreground request queue grows past a length threshold; it does not consider device capacity and was evaluated only on read-heavy traces. Workload-predictive schedulers exist for server-class SSDs. We do not evaluate them because they need more memory than our target devices have.

2. METHOD
Every 5-second window, TidalLog computes w, the bytes written by the foreground in that window, and divides by S, an exponentially weighted moving average (alpha = 0.2) of the device throughput measured during compaction bursts. The smoothed ratio is the tide T. When T is above 0.7 (high tide), compaction of level 2 and deeper is deferred, for at most 3 consecutive windows (15 seconds). When T is below 0.3 (low tide), compaction is advanced: the level with the highest overlap score is compacted opportunistically. Level 0 is exempt: it compacts once it holds 8 files, and writes stall at 12 files. The implementation is about 2,900 lines of C++17 on top of MicroLSM, our in-house open-source store. The thresholds 0.7 and 0.3 were chosen by grid search (0.5 to 0.9 and 0.1 to 0.4) on workload W-B only.

3. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Hardware: quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 at 1.4 GHz, 2 GB RAM, 32 GB eMMC 5.1. Workloads: W-A write-heavy (80% writes), W-B balanced (50% writes), W-C read-heavy (5% writes). Each workload issues 64 million operations with 16-byte keys and 240-byte values under a Zipfian key distribution (theta = 0.9). Each configuration was run 5 times and we report means. We compare StaticLevel, LazyTier, BurstGuard and TidalLog.

4. RESULTS
Table 1. Main results (means of 5 runs)
System | Write amplification (W-A) | p99 read latency, ms (W-B) | Throughput, kops/s (W-A)
StaticLevel | 14.2 | 9.8 | 18.4
LazyTier | 9.7 | 14.6 | 21.9
BurstGuard | 12.5 | 8.9 | 19.1
TidalLog | 9.4 | 7.7 | 22.6

Run-to-run standard deviation was at most 0.4 for write amplification and 0.6 ms for p99 latency. On W-C, p99 read latency was within 3% across all four systems. Over the W-A run, StaticLevel performed 1.92 million block erases and TidalLog 1.27 million. Sensitivity to the smoothing factor: alpha = 0.1 gave write amplification 9.9, alpha = 0.2 gave 9.4, alpha = 0.4 gave 9.6. Crash consistency: we injected 200 power losses during W-B; every run recovered with no acknowledged write lost.

5. LIMITATIONS
We used one board and one storage type (eMMC); we did not evaluate NVMe or SD cards. Workloads are synthetic with fixed value sizes. The tide thresholds were tuned on W-B and not re-tuned per workload. Five runs per configuration is a small sample and we report no formal significance tests. We did not study multi-tenant setups or wear beyond 64 million operations. Deferral of up to 15 seconds can let compaction debt build up under sustained bursts.

6. CONCLUSION
TidalLog is a low-overhead scheduler that lowers write amplification and tail latency on flash-backed embedded stores without changing the on-disk format. Future work includes per-level thresholds and multi-device setups.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What did the report say about how much students enjoyed using it?
items.answer: The report doesn't report enjoyment or any student satisfaction measure. What it does report on engagement is usage: students in the Full condition completed a median of 24 sessions, 71% completed at least 20, and the median session length was 9 minutes. If you want how students felt about using it, that isn't in the report.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: How did you assign students to the different conditions?
items.answer: Students were randomised individually within each section, so every section had all four conditions and assignment wasn't done at the section level. That's in the study design section of the technical report.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: How sure are you?
conversation: EXAMINER (heard): So what was the main result?

NATIVELY: I don't have the specifics of the result in front of me, so I don't want to give you a number I can't stand behind. What I can tell you is what I'd point to: the headline finding, the size of the effect, and whether it held up under the checks we ran. Let me pull the exact figures and walk you through them.
items.answer: I'm confident about the shape of the finding and which checks it held up under, but I won't put a confidence number on the exact figures until I've pulled them up. Let me get those in front of us and I'll tell you exactly how much weight I'd put on each one.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Building on that, did your data show anything similar, like fewer escaped defects when two people reviewed a PR instead of one?
conversation: EXAMINER: Can I add something from the floor? At my previous company we cut escaped defects by about forty percent just by requiring a second reviewer on every PR.
EXAMINER: That is a big number. I wonder if the same thing would hold at Quillon.
items.answer: No, that's not something the data can answer. Every PR in the set had at least one reviewer, and the number of reviewers per PR wasn't recorded, so I can't compare one reviewer against two. What the study does show is that long waits for first review are associated with more escaped defects, and that PR size is the strongest single predictor.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Check this before I say it: there were sixty villages, a text went out every Tuesday, and the benefit lasted a full year. Which parts hold up and which do not, according to the deck?
items.answer: Two of the three hold up. The deck says 60 villages, 30 per arm, and the reminder arm got one SMS every Tuesday at 17:00 for 26 weeks. The benefit ran 26 weeks, not a full year, so that part doesn't hold.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What was the baseline fuel consumption per hundred kilometres?
items.answer: The baseline was **41.2 litres per 100 km**, on slide 5, against 32.6 in the trial.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Share of the fleet?
conversation: EXAMINER: The fitting was at Millgate, I think you said.
EXAMINER (heard): How many buses got the retrofit?
NATIVELY: 48 buses at Millgate were fitted, from slide 2 of the deck. The analysis itself covered 42 of them, since buses with telematics faults were excluded.
items.answer: 48 of Tarnbrook's 120 buses, so **40% of the fleet**, from slide 2 of the deck. That's the fitted share at Millgate. The analysis itself covered 42 buses, which is **35% of the fleet**.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What write amplification did TidalLog get on the read-heavy workload?
items.answer: The paper doesn't report a write amplification figure for the read-heavy workload. Table 1 gives write amplification only for W-A, the write-heavy workload, where TidalLog came in at 9.4. For W-C, the read-heavy workload, the results section reports p99 read latency, which was within 3% across all four systems, and no write amplification number.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: So adaptation on its own explains the gain?
conversation: USER (spoken): So that is the ablation table.
EXAMINER (heard): Which mattered more, the adaptation or the confidence prompts?

NATIVELY: The adaptation mattered more. Removing it cost 3.9 points, 57% of the total gain, and that was significant. Removing the confidence prompts cost 1.3 points, 19% of the gain, and that wasn't.
items.answer: Not on its own, no. Adaptation is the larger share at 57% of the gain, but the confidence prompts still account for 19%, and the two together are what the Full condition adds over Control. The honest caveat is that difficulty matching and expanding intervals were removed together in the No adaptation condition, so the ablation can't separate their contributions.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Flag anything in my slides that the paper does not support.
items.answer:
I can't flag anything yet, because no slides or paper are attached to this session. Nothing was searched, so I have no content to compare.

If you attach the deck and the paper, I'll go through the slides and point out each claim the paper doesn't support, with the slide and the section it should map to.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What was your sample size and how did you decide on it?
items.answer: I don't have the exact figure in front of me, so I won't guess at it. What I can tell you is how I got there: I sized it against the effect I needed to detect, not against what was convenient to collect, and I set the threshold before I looked at the results so the number wasn't something I could tune afterward. Let me pull the exact count and the power calculation and send them to you right after this.

conversation: USER (spoken): So that is the ablation table.
items.answer: The adaptation mattered more. Removing it cost 3.9 points, 57% of the total gain, and that was significant. Removing the confidence prompts cost 1.3 points, 19% of the gain, and that wasn't.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: How long did the trial run for?
items.answer: The trial ran six months, February to July 2024, on Route family 14 with 48 buses fitted at Millgate. One thing to flag: the results table lists the trial dates as 1 February to 30 September 2024, so the deck isn't consistent on the end date, and I'd want to confirm which is right before quoting it.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What does the deck say about the villages far from a clinic?
items.answer: The deck reports that in villages more than 5 km from a clinic, the risk ratio was **0.61** (0.42 to 0.89), while in villages 5 km or less away it was 0.83 (0.58 to 1.19). That's from slide 8, and it's flagged as exploratory: the interaction p was 0.21 and it was not a pre-registered confirmatory comparison. Distance to the nearest clinic was also the stratification variable in the design on slide 4.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What hardware?
items.answer: The hardware was a quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 at 1.4 GHz, with 2 GB of RAM and 32 GB of eMMC 5.1 storage. That's the setup in the experimental section of the paper, and all three workloads ran on it.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Why did that happen?
conversation: EXAMINER: Quick update: the integration slipped by about two weeks. The vendor changed their API without telling us.
EXAMINER: Right. And the original date was already tight.
items.answer: The vendor changed their API without telling us, so the integration slipped by about two weeks. That's the whole of it on our side. What I'd want to pin down now is whether they gave any notice at all, and whether the original date still holds.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: What does the deck say about whether households actually read the messages, and what does it leave out?
items.answer:
The deck says the SMS gateway logged **91% of messages as delivered**, but it states plainly that it could not verify that messages were read. So delivery is documented, reading is not.

What it leaves out is any measure of actual exposure or engagement: no read receipts, no self-reported recall of the messages, and no check on whether households acted on the three instructions. The limitations slide doesn't list this either, so the gap between "delivered" and "read" isn't flagged as a limitation in the deck.

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Can you explain that?
items.answer: I'd be glad to, but I'm not sure which part you mean. Could you point to the specific slide or claim you'd like me to walk through?

items.role: USER: the presenter / researcher defending their work. OTHER PARTY: examiner / audience. Natively: the presenter's answer, grounded in the attached material.
items.question: Only about eighty percent took the delayed quiz. Doesn't that undermine the retention result?
items.answer: Eighty percent is the completion rate, and the retention result is reported on the students who took the delayed quiz, so the number itself doesn't change the outcome. What it does mean is that the result describes that group rather than the whole cohort, and I'd want to check whether the students who skipped differ in a way that matters before treating it as representative.
